For elements of order >= 3 we can show that they can be represented as a product of two involutions. [Proof: Write down the reduced cycle representation of the element. Decompose each sub-cycle of order >=3 into a product of two involutions, and distribute/merge the 1 or 2 factors of the involutions. For sub-cycles of order o>=3 it suffices to show that the reduced cycle (1 2 3 4 ... o), equivalent to the 1-line representation (2 3 4 .. o 1), can be written as a product of 2 involutions, because other cycles are mapped to such a product by a fixed permutation. A constructive proof here is: the reduced cycle (1 2 3 4 ... o) is the product of the two involutions (1 2)(3 o)(4 o-1)(5 o-2)... and (2 o)(3 o-1)... The first involution swaps the first two elements and reverts the ordering of all others from the 3rd on, then the second involution reverts the order of the elements from the 2nd on. The net effect is a cyclic shift of the o elements.] - _R. J. Mathar_, Jan 04 2017

conj: Conjecture: a(n) = 2^(1-n)*Product_{j=1..n} (prime(j)-1) for n >= 0, so a(n) = a(n-1)*(prime(n)-1)/2 for n >= 1.
why: Conjecture is true. Since there exists a prime congruent to r modulo 4*primorial(n) for any r coprime to primorial(n), this set is precisely the set of coprime quadratic residues of 4*primorial(n). If n >= 1, each residue can be broken down into congruences modulo 8 and the first n-1 odd primes, each odd prime p has (p-1)/2 residue classes, and every combination eventually occurs, giving the formula. (End)

conj: Conjecture: a(n) = a(n+1) if and only if n == 2 (mod 4). Verified for n <= 998.
why: Proof of the formula a(2^k+1) = 2^(2^k) - 1: by Lucas's theorem the ANF coefficient at degree d is the parity of the number of submasks j of d with j <= 2^(k-1); that number is 2^w + [bit k-1 of d is set], where w counts the bits of d in positions 0..k-2, so the coefficient is 1 exactly for d in {0, 2^k} together with 2^(k-1) < d < 2^k. Summing binomial(2^k+1, d) over that set gives 2^(2^k) by the symmetry of the binomial row, and removing the term d = 0 gives the formula.
